Contents 1 Goal and Summary 2 Starting the game 3 Turn Structure 3.1 Advance on a cruise 3.1.1 Day in Space 3.1.2 Day at Destination 3.1.3 Return to Earth 3.2 (Option 1) Taking two actions 3.3 (Option 2) Call a meeting 3.4 (Option 3) Launch your ship 3.5 (End Of Turn Extra) Check for achievements 4 Actions 4.1 Get Resources / Ads 4.1.1 Action - Buy resources and ads 4.1.2 Action - Get for free from the silo 4.1.3 Action - Replenish one type of good in the silo 4.2 Build a ship 4.2.1 Action - Get a new ship 4.2.2 Action - Get Blueprints 4.2.3 Action - Build ship segments 4.3 Schedule/advertise a cruise 4.3.1 Action - Schedule a cruise 4.3.2 Action - Advertise a cruise 4.4 Upgrades and improvements 4.4.1 Action - Buy a Development (Gears) 4.4.2 Action - Hire an expert worker 4.4.3 Action - Get agenda cards 4.4.4 Action - Refill agenda cards 5 Launching your ship 5.1 Choose a pilot 5.2 Add guests to the ship 5.3 Pay resources 5.4 Start the cruise 6 End of game 7 References 8 BGA Limitations and special rules 8.1 Resolve Delayed Bump 8.2 Rachel's choices 8.3 Anytime actions 8.4 Agenda cards with pre-requisites 8.5 Agenda: COLLABORATION 8.6 Agenda: STRATEGIC RELATIONSHIP Goal and Summary The goal of Galactic Cruise is to get the most points during the game. You can do this from connecting your campus network, building your ship, visiting cruise destinations, and more! On your turn, you'll usually be taking two actions at a campus building (or one nearby) to help prepare for your galactic cruise. Once you're ready, you can liftoff and visit stops on your cruise schedule for points and resource while you prepare for the next one. After a certain number of launches and achievements among all players, the game will end with players finishing up, and then most points wins! Starting the game Each player will start by picking some blueprints and also put out their gear between two buildings. (If this is your first game, feel free to just pick something!) Turn Structure Advance on a cruise Only applicable if you already launched a ship. (This step usually only happens later in the game.) Move your ship one day forward on the schedule, and do that day: Day in Space If you move to a space symbol, multiply the number of orange guests on the cruise times the number of orange tags on your cruise ship components, then receive the orange guest bonus that many times. (Guest bonuses are listed top right corner of the campus map.) Repeat for purple and teal guests. Day at Destination If you land on a orange, purple, or teal space (a planet), you can first optionally deliver your upgrade token to get one of three upgrades at the destination. You must pay ads for each guest you want to score - 1 ad for each that matches the destination color, and 2 ads for each that doesn't. Each one you pay for scores 3 points, plus 1 for each upgrade token at that destination. Return to Earth On last day on each schedule, guests return to earth (back to the supply), cruise is returned to discard, pilot is return to break room (gets a funding bonus) and ship can be used again. (Option 1) Taking two actions Pick a worker to send to one of the six stations. If it already has another player's worker, you can bump it back to that player, giving them a funding bonus. (You can't bump your own worker though, unless you unlock such upgrade) You can take two actions (same or different) as follows An action at your building An action at an adjacent building connected by a gear of yours. An action at an adjacent building connected by at least one opponent's gear, if you pay 0-2 Money to every opponent that has a gear. [Rating: 1/10] Eurostew that has Lacerda echoes.  +Iconography takes work but once internalised gives a lot of information, game presents nicely on table. –Will require a hefty teach (like 30 minutes for new players), recommend Grogan's how to play video.   –MPS little interaction, too much heads down staring at your own personal player board. –Unbalanced Agenda cards are a dollop of randomness. Some are super!  –Long given obvious decision pathways.   –Point salad, everything gives points. xKickout secondary action has the same issue as The Gallerist, the more times you get kicked out the better.

[Rating: 1/10] Here we go again with another Euro multi-player solitaire game. It's glossy and has a cool theme, but it's a re-hash of other point-salad Euros, complete with a point track on the edge of the board. I was in a 4-player game and I never felt like I was playing with or against the other players, nevermind the long lag between taking turns. Took 3+ hours to play and I think I got a total of 20 min "playing time" in. [Rating: 1/10] Another bloated eurogame doing bloated eurogame things. Despite what at a glance appears to be a breadth of available options, players inevitably fall into a loop of doing the same things over and over again. The variable aspects don't offer as much dissimilitude as one would expect or hope (i.e., the differences between the massive sack of blueprints, for one example, are minimal when considering that you can easily get any types of passengers you want and any cruise locations you desire because there are a ton available at any given moment). [Rating: 1/10] Way too much iconography, too many corner case actions, the action loop is way too long and convoluted. A bloated, head-down mess. Not worth the time investment to learn  the strategy to play again.

[Rating: 2/10] Not for me - too complicated and you never know what's going on and it has player boards full of bits and pieces.

[Rating: 2/10] Galactic Cruise is beautiful, tantalising and ultimately underwhelming.   Its a lattice of interlocking systems that somehow all feel much the same – perfunctory, administrative, dull. Its decision space is computational, rather than tactical or strategic. Its complexity is engineered, rather than emergent – persnickety rules and bloated systems, rather than players' interactions and incentives.  Part of the problem is that Galactic Cruise is too forgiving. You can play to almost any space, take almost any action, and pay almost any resource. However, I really like the “cruise” mechanism and how it functions from start to finish. Overall, it felt like the best Lacerda-style game I’ve played—clearly inspired by Kanban.  Updated Thoughts (After Second Play): After a second playthrough, I’m not as impressed. I’ve revised my rating from a 7 to a 5. [Rating: 3/10] Too many not very meaningful decisions, which contribute to a play time which is far longer than necessary. It would be much improved by reducing some of the kinds of tiles (e.g. the middle ship segments) to just a handful of meaningfully different options which are always available.  It also has very little interaction. I prefer games with more interaction, and especially in games of this length.
